en.title: The Max Height Arc
en.narration: Welcome to Projectile Motion. Today we master The Max Height Arc. According to NCERT: At maximum height, the vertical component of velocity is zero while horizontal velocity remains v0*cos(theta). The primary formula is: H max = (v naught squared * sin^2(θ)) / (2g). Notice this crucial insight: HCV Ch 3: Speed at the top is not zero; it equals v0*cos(theta). Kinetic energy is minimum but non-zero. Pay special attention to this NEET trap point: Confusing total velocity being zero with only vertical velocity component being zero at top of trajectory. Keep this core relationship firmly in mind to secure top marks in NEET.

en.title: Time of Flight
en.narration: Welcome to Projectile Motion. Today we master Time of Flight. According to NCERT: Time of flight is determined purely by the vertical component of initial velocity. The primary formula is: T = (2 * v naught squared * sin(θ)) / g. Notice this crucial insight: HCV Ch 3: The horizontal velocity component vx has zero acceleration and does not affect the time spent in the air. Pay special attention to this NEET trap point: Question specifies angle with vertical axis instead of horizontal (swapping sin with cos). Keep this core relationship firmly in mind to secure top marks in NEET.

en.title: Horizontal Range and Complementary Angles
en.narration: Welcome to Projectile Motion. Today we master Horizontal Range and Complementary Angles. According to NCERT: Horizontal range is identical for complementary projection angles theta and (90 - theta) at the same initial speed. The primary formula is: R = (v naught squared * sin(2θ)) / g. Notice this crucial insight: HCV Ch 3: Although ranges are equal for theta and 90-theta, maximum heights and times of flight are strictly unequal. Pay special attention to this NEET trap point: Assuming time of flight and maximum height are also equal when ranges are equal for complementary angles. Keep this core relationship firmly in mind to secure top marks in NEET.

en.title: Equation of Trajectory
en.narration: Welcome to Projectile Motion. Today we master Equation of Trajectory. According to NCERT: The trajectory of a projectile is parabolic in nature, relating vertical coordinate y to horizontal coordinate x. The primary formula is: y = x*tan(θ) - (g*x^2) / (2*v naught squared*cos^2(θ)). Notice this crucial insight: HCV Ch 3: Alternative formulation y = x*tan(theta)*(1 - x/R) simplifies range-based NEET problems instantly. Pay special attention to this NEET trap point: Confusing tan(theta) factor with cot(theta) when comparing experimental trajectory equations. Keep this core relationship firmly in mind to secure top marks in NEET.

en.title: Centripetal Acceleration
en.narration: Welcome to Uniform Circular Motion. Today we master Centripetal Acceleration. According to NCERT: Acceleration in uniform circular motion always points radially inward toward the center of the circle. The primary formula is: a_c = v^2 / r = omega^2 * r. Notice this crucial insight: HCV Ch 7: Speed is constant but velocity continuously changes direction; therefore acceleration is non-zero and perpendicular to velocity. Pay special attention to this NEET trap point: Assuming acceleration is zero because speed is constant in uniform circular motion. Keep this core relationship firmly in mind to secure top marks in NEET.

en.title: Position-Time Graphs

en.title: Resolution of Vectors

en.title: Horizontal Range and Complementary Angles
en.narration: Welcome to Projectile Motion. Today we master Horizontal Range and Complementary Angles. According to NCERT: Horizontal range is identical for complementary projection angles theta and (90 - theta) at the same initial speed. The primary formula is: R = (v naught squared * sin(2θ)) / g. en.title: Equation of Trajectory
en.narration: Welcome to Projectile Motion. Today we master Equation of Trajectory. According to NCERT: The trajectory of a projectile is parabolic in nature, relating vertical coordinate y to horizontal coordinate x. The primary formula is: y = x*tan(θ) - (g*x^2) / (2*v naught squared*cos^2(θ)). Notice this crucial insight: HCV Ch 3: Alternative formulation y = x*tan(theta)*(1 - x/R) simplifies range-based NEET problems instantly. Pay special attention to this NEET trap point: Confusing tan(theta) factor with cot(theta) when comparing experimental trajectory equations. Keep this core relationship firmly in mind to secure top marks in NEET. Up next in video 7: Centripetal Acceleration.

en.title: Centripetal Acceleration
en.narration: Welcome to Uniform Circular Motion. Today we master Centripetal Acceleration. According to NCERT: Acceleration in uniform circular motion always points radially inward toward the center of the circle. The primary formula is: a_c = v^2 / r = omega^2 * r. Notice this crucial insight: HCV Ch 7: Speed is constant but velocity continuously changes direction; therefore acceleration is non-zero and perpendicular to velocity. Pay special attention to this NEET trap point: Assuming acceleration is zero because speed is constant in uniform circular motion. Keep this core relationship firmly in mind to secure top marks in NEET. Up next in video 8: Banking of Roads.
